title: Turnus as a wounded lion
greek: Poenorum qualis in arvis / saucius ille gravi venantum vulnere pectus / tum demum movet arma leo
short: The last book opens with Turnus, burning to fight, compared to an African lion that has been wounded by hunters and only then rouses itself.
body: The book begins not with Aeneas but with Turnus, seen through a simile. Conington and Nettleship identify two Homeric models: Diomedes, wounded and fighting with tripled fury like a lion grazed by a shepherd (Iliad 5.134-43), and Achilles advancing against Aeneas like a lion attacked by a whole village (Iliad 20.164-73). They note that the localisation 'in the fields of the Carthaginians' is Virgil's own; the African setting may recall Carthage and Dido, another enemy of Aeneas' mission. The lion is already wounded (saucius), and breaks the hunter's spear while roaring with bloody mouth: a picture of courage that is also of defeat foreseen. The word 'implacabilis' and the image of rising fury (ardet, attollit animos) establish the violence that will drive the whole book.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 406, note on 12.4

title: Lavinia's blush
greek: Indum sanguineo veluti violaverit ostro / si quis ebur, aut mixta rubent ubi lilia multa / alba rosa
short: Hearing her mother's plea, Lavinia blushes deeply, like ivory stained with crimson or white lilies mixed with roses; Turnus is thrown into turmoil by love.
body: Lavinia never speaks in the Aeneid, and this blush is her one strongly marked reaction. Conington and Nettleship trace the simile to Iliad 4.141-7, where Menelaus' blood running down his thigh is compared to ivory that a Maeonian or Carian woman stains with purple; they note that 'Indum ebur' is Virgil's own localisation and that 'violaverit' (has violated, stained) is used because purple is not ivory's natural colour, adding that the word may carry a modern sentimental tone not present in Homer. The cause of the blush is left open, and readers have argued about it ever since: love for Turnus, modesty at being discussed in public, distress at her mother's threat to die, or simply the conventional beauty of an epic bride. What is clear is its effect on Turnus: 'illum turbat amor', love throws him into tumult, and he burns the more for battle.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 411, note on 12.67
R. J. Tarrant, Virgil: Aeneid Book XII (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012), notes on 12.64-9

title: Turnus' insult: 'the effeminate Phrygian'
greek: da sternere corpus / loricamque manu valida lacerare revulsam / semiviri Phrygis et foedare in pulvere crinis / vibratos calido ferro murraque madentis
short: Addressing his spear, Turnus prays to strip and kill the 'half-man Phrygian' and to foul in the dust his hair, curled with hot irons and dripping with myrrh.
body: The insult belongs to a series in which Italians and Africans sneer at the Trojans as soft easterners: Iarbas mocks Aeneas as 'that Paris' with his Lydian bonnet and perfumed hair (4.215-17), and Numanus taunts the Trojans with their saffron, dances and turbans (9.614-20). Conington and Nettleship cross-refer to 4.215-16, explain 'vibratos' as curled (citing Pliny), and compare Ovid's 'madidus murra crinis'; they note that 'foedare in pulvere' recalls Homer, where Patroclus' helmet is fouled with blood and dust (Iliad 16.795-6). The stereotype of 'Phrygian' effeminacy was familiar at Rome; Virgil puts it in the mouth of Aeneas' enemies while letting Diomedes, who fought him, praise his courage and pietas (11.282-92). Turnus' wish to defile Aeneas' corpse is answered by his own death.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 414, note on 12.99 and 12.100

title: Juno on the Alban Mount
greek: at Iuno e summo (qui nunc Albanus habetur; / tum neque nomen erat neque honos aut gloria monti) / prospiciens tumulo
short: Juno watches from the hill later called the Alban Mount, which at this time had 'neither name, nor honour, nor glory'.
body: The Alban Mount (Monte Cavo), south-east of Rome, overlooks the plain where the treaty is to be sworn. Virgil's parenthesis looks forward: here Ascanius will found Alba Longa, the line of Alban kings will rule (1.267-74), and the mountain will become the seat of Jupiter Latiaris, where the Latins held their common festival (feriae Latinae). Such 'it was not yet' remarks are a favourite device of Virgil's (compare the site of Rome in 8.347-61). Conington and Nettleship observe that the Alban Mount serves Virgil's battle as Ida serves Homer's, and compare Hera watching from Gargarus, the peak of Ida (Iliad 14.292-3), and Zeus on Ida (8.47-52). Juno's viewpoint over a future Roman landscape adds irony to her last attempt to block the Trojans.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 417, note on 12.134

title: Juturna, Turnus' sister
greek: diva deam, stagnis quae fluminibusque sonoris / praesidet (hunc illi rex aetheris altus honorem / Iuppiter erepta pro virginitate sacravit)
short: Turnus' sister is a nymph of pools and rivers, made immortal by Jupiter in return for her lost virginity; Juno urges her to save her brother or wreck the treaty.
body: Juturna was a real Roman deity of springs. Servius explains that she was a very healthy spring in Italy near the river Numicus, her name derived from iuvare (to help), since her waters healed; Conington and Nettleship add that a lake of Juturna was fed by a stream from the Alban Mount. At Rome the spring of Juturna (lacus Iuturnae) in the Forum was associated with Castor and Pollux. Virgil makes her Turnus' sister and gives her a bitter history: Jupiter raped her and paid her with immortality and power over waters. Juno's address 'diva deam' (goddess to goddess) is modelled, Conington notes, on a phrase in Odyssey 5, where Hermes speaks to Calypso as 'god to goddess'. Juturna is the active force of the first half of Book XII: she incites the Rutulians, sends the false omen, and drives Turnus' chariot as Metiscus, until the Fury forces her to leave him (12.869-86).

sources.cite: Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.139
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 418, note on 12.139
R. J. Tarrant, Virgil: Aeneid Book XII (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012), notes on 12.134-60

title: Latinus' crown of twelve rays
greek: cui tempora circum / aurati bis sex radii fulgentia cingunt, / Solis avi specimen
short: Latinus rides to the treaty in a four-horse chariot wearing a radiate crown, a sign of his descent from the Sun.
body: The 'twelve golden rays' form a radiate crown, the attribute of the Sun-god. Servius explains 'Solis avi specimen' (token of his grandfather the Sun) by the Hesiodic tradition that Latinus was the son of Ulysses and Circe, who is the daughter of the Sun (compare Hesiod, Theogony 1011-13, where Circe bears Agrius and Latinus to Odysseus); he adds that Virgil varies his genealogies, since in 7.47-9 Latinus is son of Faunus and grandson of Picus. Conington and Nettleship compare Apollonius' description of Circe, whose descent from the Sun showed in the golden light of her eyes (Argonautica 4.727-9). The radiate crown was also worn by Hellenistic kings, and later appears on Roman imperial coins. The pomp of Latinus contrasts with Turnus' simple pair of white horses and two spears, and with Aeneas in his 'starry shield and heavenly arms'.

sources.cite: Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.164
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 420, note on 12.162 and 12.163-164

title: The treaty sacrifice
greek: pura ... in veste sacerdos / saetigeri fetum suis intonsamque bidentem / attulit ... dant fruges manibus salsas et tempora ferro / summa notant pecudum
short: A priest in spotless robes brings a young pig and an unshorn two-year-old sheep; the leaders face the sunrise, sprinkle salted meal, mark the victims and pour libations.
body: Virgil follows Roman ritual closely. Conington and Nettleship note that a pig was the ordinary victim in making a treaty (compare 8.641, and Livy 1.24, where the fetial strikes the pig with a flint), and explain 'pura veste' as clothing without stain or mourning, citing Festus. 'Bidens' is a sheep of the age when it shows two prominent teeth. Servius explains the 'salted fruits' as far and salt (the mola salsa), sprinkled on the knives and the victims, and the marking of the brows with the knife as part of the preliminary tests of the animal's fitness, the blade being drawn from forehead to tail before the killing. Facing the rising sun (12.172) suits an oath sworn by the Sun. The careful description of a correctly performed rite makes the breaking of the treaty soon after all the more sacrilegious.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 420, note on 12.169, 12.170 and 12.172
Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.173
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. bidens

title: Aeneas' terms: two unconquered nations under equal laws
greek: non ego nec Teucris Italos parere iubebo / nec mihi regna peto: paribus se legibus ambae / invictae gentes aeterna in foedera mittant
short: Aeneas swears that if he wins he will not make Italy subject to the Trojans: both peoples, unconquered, will unite under equal laws, Latinus keeping arms and authority.
body: Aeneas' oath sets out the political settlement the poem looks forward to. If Turnus wins, the Trojans will withdraw to Evander's city; if Aeneas wins, there will be no conquest: Aeneas will give the gods and rites (sacra deosque dabo), Latinus as father-in-law will keep arms and 'customary command', and the new city will be named Lavinium after Lavinia. Conington and Nettleship explain 'paribus legibus' as government on terms of equality, 'not one as a conquered, one as a conquering people', and compare Juno's proposal of a shared rule in 4.102-3. Many readers connect this ideal union of Trojans and Italians with the politics of Virgil's own time, when the Italian peoples had only recently won Roman citizenship after the Social War (91-88 BC); this is an interpretation, not something the text states. The terms are fulfilled in Jupiter's settlement with Juno (12.834-40).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 422, note on 12.190

title: Latinus' oath by the sceptre; Janus
greek: ut sceptrum hoc (dextra sceptrum nam forte gerebat) / numquam fronde levi fundet virgulta nec umbras
short: Latinus swears by gods of earth, sea, sky and underworld, including two-faced Janus, and seals the oath by his sceptre, which will never sprout again.
body: The sceptre oath translates Achilles' oath in Iliad 1.234-9: as this staff, cut from the tree and bound in bronze, will never again put out leaves, so surely will I keep my word. Conington and Nettleship note the imitation and Wagner's remark that the comparison is strange, since the two things compared share nothing except that neither will happen. Servius explains why a sceptre was used: in treaties the ancients produced an image of Jupiter, and when this became cumbersome, especially with distant peoples, a sceptre held in the hand served instead, so that Latinus holds it not as king but as pater patratus, the fetial priest who swore for the state. Servius also says Janus is rightly invoked because he presides over treaties: his two-faced image was made after Romulus and Titus Tatius joined their peoples. Latinus' oath is kept; the Rutulians break the truce within minutes.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 424, note on 12.206
Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.206
Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.198

title: The false omen of the eagle and the swan
greek: namque volans rubra fulvus Iovis ales in aethra / litoreas agitabat avis turbamque sonantem / agminis aligeri
short: Juturna sends a deceptive sign: Jupiter's eagle seizes a swan, the other birds mob it and force it to drop its prey; the augur Tolumnius reads this as Aeneas' defeat.
body: The eagle is Jupiter's bird, and bird-signs were the basis of Roman augury. Tolumnius interprets: the eagle is the 'greedy stranger' Aeneas, the birds who rescue the swan are the united Rutulians, and he hurls the spear that breaks the truce, killing one of nine Arcadian brothers. Conington and Nettleship point to the Homeric model, Iliad 12.200-29, where an eagle carrying a serpent is bitten and drops it among the Trojans; Polydamas reads it as a warning, but Hector rejects it and says 'one omen is best, to fight for one's country'. Virgil's omen is explicitly 'fallax', sent by Juturna to confuse Italian minds. Its true sense, if any, is debated: some read it as a foreshadowing of the end, when Aeneas (the eagle) loses only a little before triumphing. Tolumnius himself dies soon after (12.460-1).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 427, note on 12.247

title: The arrow from an unknown hand
greek: ecce viro stridens alis adlapsa sagitta est, / incertum qua pulsa manu, quo turbine adacta, / quis tantam Rutulis laudem, casusne deusne, / attulerit
short: As Aeneas, bareheaded and unarmed, tries to stop the fighting and keep the treaty, an arrow from no one knows whom wounds him.
body: Aeneas' behaviour here, holding out an unarmed hand and calling 'mine alone is the right of battle', is a model of the treaty-keeper. The wound that follows has no author: 'chance or god', and no one boasted of it, so that 'the fame of the great deed was suppressed'. The scene answers the truce-breaking in Iliad 4.86-140, where Athena prompts Pandarus to shoot Menelaus during a truce, an arrow whose archer is well known. Conington and Nettleship note the parallel phrase 'alis adlapsa sagitta' at 9.578 and the readings in 12.321. The anonymity may suggest divine agency (Juno later swears by the Styx that she did not cause 'the arrow-shot', 12.815-16) or the general guilt of the side that broke faith. The wound takes Aeneas off the field, leaves room for Turnus' aristeia, and leads to the healing scene.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 433, note on 12.319, 12.320 and 12.321

title: Iapyx, the healer who chose a silent art
greek: iamque aderat Phoebo ante alios dilectus Iapyx / Iasides ... ille ut depositi proferret fata parentis, / scire potestates herbarum usumque medendi / maluit et mutas agitare inglorius artis
short: Apollo offered his favourite Iapyx prophecy, the lyre and archery; he chose medicine instead, to prolong his dying father's life, a 'silent art without glory'.
body: Iapyx is a small figure with a moving biography. Offered Apollo's glamorous gifts, he chose healing, the humblest of the god's arts, out of pietas towards his father. Conington and Nettleship discuss the spelling (the best manuscripts give Iapyx or Iapix, though Heyne preferred Iapis) and explain his robe girt 'in Paeonian fashion' (Paeonium in morem) as 'in the manner of physicians', with Servius: Paeon was the physician of the gods in Homer (Iliad 5.401-2, 899-901). Despite his skill and the 'powerful herbs of Phoebus', he cannot extract the arrowhead; Apollo does not help, and the healing must come from Venus. Iapyx himself recognises it: 'this comes not by human means ... a greater god is at work'. The scene follows Homeric scenes of battlefield surgery, such as Patroclus tending Eurypylus (Iliad 11.828-48).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 439, note on 12.391 and 12.401

title: Dittany of Crete
greek: dictamnum genetrix Cretaea carpit ab Ida, / puberibus caulem foliis et flore comantem / purpureo; non illa feris incognita capris / gramina, cum tergo volucres haesere sagittae
short: Venus picks dittany on Cretan Ida, the herb wild goats eat to expel arrows, and secretly adds it with ambrosia and panacea to the water that heals Aeneas.
body: Dittany (Origanum dictamnus), a downy-leaved herb growing on the mountains of Crete, was believed in antiquity to draw out weapons from wounds. Cicero reports that wild goats in Crete, when struck by poisoned arrows, seek out the herb called dictamnus, and that when they eat it the arrows fall out of their bodies (De natura deorum 2.126); Aristotle and Pliny tell the same story. Conington and Nettleship record that Tiberius Donatus read 'ipsa manu' instead of 'dictamnum' in 12.412, and they discuss the reading. Venus adds ambrosia and fragrant 'panacea' ('all-heal'). The cure is instantaneous: the pain leaves, the blood stops, the arrow falls out 'following the hand'. Iapyx, who bathes the wound unknowing, recognises divine help. Mackail's 'dittamy' is an old English spelling of the plant's name.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 441, note on 12.412
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. dictamnus

title: 'Disce, puer, virtutem ex me': Aeneas to Ascanius
greek: disce, puer, virtutem ex me verumque laborem, / fortunam ex aliis
short: Armed again, Aeneas kisses Ascanius through his helmet: 'learn courage and true toil from me, good fortune from others'; let him remember Aeneas and his uncle Hector.
body: Aeneas' words to his son here are a farewell before possible death, and the only extended address to him in the closing books. Conington and Nettleship note that Virgil is probably thinking of the famous words of Sophocles' Ajax to his son Eurysaces, 'be luckier than your father, but in all else like him' (Ajax 550-1); 'verum laborem' means real toil, not fighting that beats the air. The scene also recalls Hector holding Astyanax and praying that he may be greater than his father (Iliad 6.466-81), where the child is frightened by the plumed helmet; here Aeneas kisses Ascanius through the helmet's visor ('summaque per oscula libans'). 'Avunculus Hector': Hector was brother of Creusa, Ascanius' mother. The bleak half-line 'fortune from others' acknowledges how little good fortune Aeneas has known, and many readers find it one of the most personal moments in his characterisation.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 443, note on 12.435-436 and 12.437

title: 'Aeterna gentis in pace futuras': the poet questions Jupiter
greek: tanton placuit concurrere motu, / Iuppiter, aeterna gentis in pace futuras?
short: The poet asks how to tell so much slaughter, and asks Jupiter whether he willed that peoples destined to eternal peace should clash so violently.
body: This is one of the few moments where Virgil speaks in his own voice to question the gods. It begins with a Homeric-style appeal for help in narrating many deaths (compare Iliad 12.176, 'it is hard for me to tell all this like a god'), then turns into a direct challenge: was it Jupiter's will that Trojans and Italians, who will form one people, should fight with such violence? Conington and Nettleship comment mainly on the text ('tanton' confirmed by Servius) and on 'motu', comparing 'magno discordia motu' in Georgics 4.68. For Roman readers the war between future fellow-citizens could suggest the civil and Italian wars of the first century BC. The question receives no answer; the narrative goes straight on to the paired killings by Aeneas and Turnus.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 449, note on 12.503

title: Amata's suicide by hanging
greek: purpureos moritura manu discindit amictus / et nodum informis leti trabe nectit ab alta
short: Believing Turnus dead, Queen Amata calls herself the cause of the evil and hangs herself from a beam, the most shameful form of death.
body: Servius, quoted by Conington and Nettleship, explains 'informis leti' (an unsightly death) from Roman religious law: it was laid down in the pontifical books that one who ended life by the noose should be thrown out unburied, so Virgil calls it the most disgraceful kind of death; he also cites Varro on the denial of funeral rites to those who hang themselves. Hanging is the death of women in Greek tragedy and myth, such as Jocasta (Odyssey 11.277-9, Sophocles' Oedipus Tyrannus), whom Conington compares. Amata cries that she is 'the cause, the guilt, the source of the evils' (causam ... crimenque caputque malorum); her death parallels Dido's, another queen destroyed by the Trojans' coming, and leads Lavinia to tear her hair and Latinus to pour dust on his head. The news helps decide Turnus to face Aeneas.

sources.cite: Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.603
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 457, note on 12.603

title: Aeneas like Athos, Eryx and Father Apennine
greek: quantus Athos aut quantus Eryx aut ipse coruscis / cum fremit ilicibus quantus gaudetque nivali / vertice se attollens pater Appenninus ad auras
short: Hearing Turnus' challenge, Aeneas leaves the siege and advances, huge as three great mountains of Greece, Sicily and Italy.
body: The three mountains map Aeneas' journey: Athos in the northern Aegean, Eryx in western Sicily (where Anchises was buried and Venus had a famous temple), and the Apennines, Italy's spine, personified as 'father Apennine' roaring with his oak-woods and lifting his snowy head. Servius, followed by Conington and Nettleship, discusses the form 'Athon', which the metre requires, and identifies Athos as a mountain near Thrace on a promontory of Macedonia and Eryx as the Sicilian mountain above Drepanum. The image recalls Hector charging 'like a snowy mountain' (Iliad 13.754). The rising scale of the comparison, ending in Italy, presents Aeneas as now belonging to the land he has come to rule.

sources.cite: Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.701
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 465, note on 12.701

title: Jupiter's scales
greek: Iuppiter ipse duas aequato examine lances / sustinet et fata imponit diversa duorum, / quem damnet labor et quo vergat pondere letum
short: As Aeneas and Turnus close, Jupiter himself holds up a balance with their two fates in the pans to see whose death weighs it down.
body: Conington and Nettleship identify the source as Iliad 22.209-13, where Zeus weighs the death-fates (kēres) of Achilles and Hector and Hector's sinks towards Hades; Homer also weighs the fates of whole armies (Iliad 8.69-74). They explain 'examen' as the tongue of the balance and 'lances' as the pans, and note that Aeschylus in his lost Psychostasia (Weighing of Souls) seems to have reversed the image, having Zeus weigh the lives, not the deaths, of Memnon and Achilles. Virgil does not report the result. Instead the next lines show Turnus' sword breaking, which tells the reader the answer. The scene recalls Jupiter's claim in Book X to leave each side to its fate (10.111-13): here he simply ascertains what fate has decided.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 467, note on 12.725-728

title: Turnus' borrowed sword shatters
greek: postquam arma dei ad Volcania ventum est, / mortalis mucro glacies ceu futtilis ictu / dissiluit
short: Turnus' sword breaks on Aeneas' divine armour: rumour says that in his haste he had taken his charioteer's sword instead of his father's, forged by Vulcan.
body: Earlier Turnus had armed with the sword Vulcan made for his father Daunus and tempered in the Styx (12.90-1). Virgil, introducing the explanation with 'fama est' (the story goes), says that when Turnus leapt into his chariot to renew the fighting after Aeneas was wounded he snatched up Metiscus' sword; Conington and Nettleship identify the moment as 12.324-7 and gloss 'mortalis' as 'made by mortal hand', in contrast to the 'Vulcanian arms'. The mortal blade shivers like brittle ice and its pieces glitter on the sand. Conington compares Iliad 16.114-18, where Hector lops the head off Ajax's spear and Ajax recognises the hand of the gods. The broken sword leaves Turnus fleeing in circles, and leads to the chase and to Juturna and Venus each restoring a weapon.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 468, note on 12.735, 12.736 and 12.740

title: The wild olive of Faunus
greek: forte sacer Fauno foliis oleaster amaris / hic steterat, nautis olim venerabile lignum, / servati ex undis ubi figere dona solebant / Laurenti divo et votas suspendere vestis
short: Aeneas' spear sticks in the stump of a wild olive sacred to Faunus, which the Trojans had cut down; Turnus prays to Faunus and Earth to hold it fast.
body: Sailors saved from shipwreck customarily dedicated their wet clothes or a votive picture to the god who saved them (Horace, Odes 1.5.13-16); here they hung them on a sacred tree of Faunus, the old Italian woodland god and father of Latinus. The Trojans, 'regardless', had cut the tree down to clear the field. Conington and Nettleship note that the oleaster probably comes from a reminiscence of the wind-swept fig-tree by which Achilles chases Hector (Iliad 22.145), that the tree was famously tough, and that it is dedicated to Faunus as the oak of 10.423 was to be dedicated to Tiber; Faunus' worship was largely in the open air. Turnus appeals to the gods whose honours the 'Aeneadae have profaned', and Faunus answers: Aeneas cannot pull the spear out until Venus intervenes. Readers have seen in the episode the cost of the Trojan settlement to native Italian religion.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 470, note on 12.766 and 12.768

title: Juno's last request: 'sit Latium'
greek: sit Latium, sint Albani per saecula reges, / sit Romana potens Itala virtute propago: / occidit, occideritque sinas cum nomine Troia
short: Juno yields, asking only that the Latins keep their name, language and dress, and that Troy and its name stay fallen.
body: Jupiter tells Juno that the end has come and forbids further resistance. She gives way and makes a request outside fate: the native Latins must not become Trojans or change their name, speech or dress; let Latium, the Alban kings and a Roman race 'strong in Italian valour' endure, and let Troy lie dead with its name. Servius explains the point: if Rome must descend from the Trojans, at least let the Trojans take the name of the Italians, so that the Romans seem sprung from Italians, not Trojans. Conington and Nettleship note that the list of Alban kings was worked out in detail only in the Augustan age, and compare Juno's speech in Horace, Odes 3.3.18-68, where she accepts Rome on condition that Troy is never rebuilt. The reconciliation removes the divine anger that began the poem (1.4, 'saevae memorem Iunonis ob iram').

sources.cite: Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.827
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 475, note on 12.826, 12.827 and 12.828

title: Jupiter's settlement: a mixed Ausonian race
greek: sermonem Ausonii patrium moresque tenebunt ... hinc genus Ausonio mixtum quod sanguine surget, / supra ire homines, supra ire deos pietate videbis, / nec gens ulla tuos aeque celebrabit honores
short: Jupiter grants Juno's wishes: Italians keep their language and customs, the Trojans merge into them, and the mixed race will excel in pietas and honour Juno.
body: Smiling, Jupiter agrees. The Trojans will 'sink' into the Italian body, contributing only their sacred rites (morem ritusque sacrorum), and all will be 'Latins of one speech'. From this mixture will rise a people who will surpass men and gods in pietas. Conington and Nettleship call 'supra ire deos' a rhetorical exaggeration, and suggest that the promise that no nation will honour Juno more may allude to Augustus' restoration of the temple of Juno Regina on the Aventine, recorded in his Res Gestae (19). The settlement realises Aeneas' oath of equal laws and answers Juno's anger, which was the cause of the whole poem. Juno 'assents and changes her mind with joy'. Yet the scene is immediately followed by Jupiter's dispatch of a Fury, which complicates any simple sense of harmony at the close.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 476, note on 12.835-837, 12.838, 12.839 and 12.840

title: The Dirae: Jupiter sends a Fury
greek: dicuntur geminae pestes cognomine Dirae, / quas et Tartaream Nox intempesta Megaeram / uno eodemque tulit partu
short: Jupiter sends one of the twin Dirae, sisters of Megaera; as a small night-bird she beats at Turnus' shield, paralysing him and driving Juturna away.
body: The Dirae ('dread ones') are Furies who wait at Jupiter's throne and carry out his punishments. Conington and Nettleship point out that in Aeschylus the Furies are shut out from the company of the Olympian gods (Eumenides 365-6), whereas here, as in Book VII, the Fury serves the upper gods; they equate 'Dirae' with the Greek Arai, 'Curses', the name the Furies give themselves in Aeschylus (Eumenides 417). The Dira descends like a poisoned arrow shot by a Parthian or Cretan archer (Conington compares Lucan on Parthian arrows) and shrinks into the shape of the small bird that sits at night on tombs and roofs, an owl; Conington discusses Servius' insistence on the little owl and Pliny's evidence that the horned owl (bubo) was a terrible omen. It is notable that Jupiter, not Juno, now uses a hellish power; Allecto, Juno's Fury in Book VII, had begun the war.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 476, note on 12.845, 12.857 and 12.862

title: Juturna's lament for her immortality
greek: haec pro virginitate reponit? / quo vitam dedit aeternam? cur mortis adempta est / condicio?
short: Recognising the Fury, Juturna leaves Turnus, lamenting that Jupiter's gift of eternal life only makes her grief eternal, and plunges into her river.
body: Juturna's speech is one of the most bitter in the poem. She recognises the 'whistling wings' and 'the proud commands of great-hearted Jupiter', and asks whether this is his payment for her virginity. Immortality now cuts her off from the one release open to mortals: she cannot follow her brother into death. Conington and Nettleship sum up the thought at 12.879: his gift of eternal life will only serve to make her grief eternal. In Homer the gods are spared lasting grief; Virgil gives a goddess the full weight of human mourning, as Venus and Juno also feel pain in this poem. She covers her head with her grey-green veil and sinks into the river, the gesture of mourning and withdrawal. Her departure leaves Turnus entirely alone for the duel.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 478, note on 12.870 and 12.879
R. J. Tarrant, Virgil: Aeneid Book XII (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012), notes on 12.869-86

title: The boundary stone
greek: saxum antiquum ingens, campo quod forte iacebat, / limes agro positus litem ut discerneret arvis
short: Turnus hurls an ancient stone that marked the boundary between fields, which twelve men of today could scarcely lift, but it falls short.
body: Conington and Nettleship identify the double model: Athena in the battle of the gods picks up a black, jagged boundary-stone set by earlier men and hurls it at Ares (Iliad 21.403-6), and Hector carries a stone that two men of a later age could hardly lift onto a wagon (Iliad 12.445-50); they also compare Iliad 5.302-4, where Aeneas himself lifts such a stone against Diomedes. 'Litem ut discerneret arvis' (to settle a dispute over land) is the language of property law; Tiberius Donatus, as they note, explains it as removing quarrels among landholders. Boundary stones were sacred at Rome, under the protection of the god Terminus. That Turnus seizes a marker of land rights in a war fought over land is a pointed image, and its failure, as his strength drains away, anticipates the end.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 481, note on 12.896-898

title: Turnus like a dreamer who cannot run
greek: ac velut in somnis, oculos ubi languida pressit / nocte quies, nequiquam avidos extendere cursus / velle videmur et in mediis conatibus aegri / succidimus
short: Under the Fury's spell Turnus is like a sleeper in a nightmare who tries in vain to run or cry out.
body: Conington and Nettleship trace the hint for this simile to Iliad 22.199-201, where Achilles chasing Hector is like a dream in which one man cannot catch the other and the other cannot escape. They also hear the rhythm and language of Lucretius' description of sleep (De rerum natura 4.453-61). Virgil turns Homer's simile, which is about both heroes, into a picture of Turnus' inner paralysis: tongue powerless, body failing, words not following. It is one of the rare similes where the poet includes himself and the reader ('we seem to want ... we sink'), drawing us into Turnus' experience at the moment he is about to lose. The 'dread goddess' (dea dira) is the Fury Jupiter has sent, so that the failure is presented both as a psychological state and as the will of heaven.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 482, note on 12.908

title: Turnus' supplication
greek: equidem merui nec deprecor ... utere sorte tua. miseri te si qua parentis / tangere cura potest, oro ... Dauni miserere senectae
short: Wounded and down, Turnus admits defeat, appeals to Aeneas by Anchises to pity old Daunus, and yields Lavinia: 'press your hatred no further'.
body: Turnus lifts 'humble eyes and a suppliant right hand'. He asks nothing for himself ('I have deserved it and I do not plead'), but appeals to Aeneas' own love for his father: 'you too had such a father in Anchises'. This echoes Priam's appeal to Achilles through the memory of Peleus (Iliad 24.486-506), the great scene of mercy in Homer. He concedes everything: 'you have won, and the Ausonians have seen me stretch out my hands in defeat; Lavinia is your wife'. The reader also remembers Anchises' charge to the Roman: 'to spare the subjected and war down the proud' (parcere subiectis et debellare superbos, 6.853). Whether Aeneas' refusal betrays or fulfils that charge is the central debate about the poem's ending; Michael Putnam's influential reading stresses the tragic violence of the close, while others defend the killing as just revenge for Pallas.

sources.cite: M. C. J. Putnam, The Poetry of the Aeneid (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1965), chapter on Book XII
R. J. Tarrant, Virgil: Aeneid Book XII (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012), introduction and notes on 12.930-52

title: The belt of Pallas decides Turnus' fate
greek: infelix umero cum apparuit alto / balteus et notis fulserunt cingula bullis / Pallantis pueri
short: As Aeneas begins to waver, he sees Pallas' sword-belt on Turnus' shoulder; inflamed with fury, he refuses mercy.
body: Aeneas stands 'fierce in arms, rolling his eyes', checks his hand, and is beginning to be moved, when the familiar studs of the belt flash on Turnus' shoulder. Conington and Nettleship explain 'infelix' as fatal, ill-omened, and point back to 10.495-505, where the narrator foretold this vengeance; with Heyne they compare the feeling in Greek tragedy that what is given by or taken from an enemy brings ill luck, recalling the Sophoclean tradition that Hector was dragged by the belt Ajax gave him and Ajax killed himself with Hector's sword. Aeneas is 'set on fire by fury and terrible in wrath' (furiis accensus et ira terribilis), language Virgil elsewhere uses of destructive passion. Readers divide over whether this is the righteous anger of pietas towards a dead ally or a final surrender to furor; Virgil gives no comment.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 484, note on 12.938 and 12.941
R. J. Tarrant, Virgil: Aeneid Book XII (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012), notes on 12.938-52

title: 'Pallas te hoc vulnere, Pallas immolat'
greek: Pallas te hoc vulnere, Pallas / immolat et poenam scelerato ex sanguine sumit
short: Aeneas kills Turnus in the name of Pallas, using the verb for sacrificing a victim: 'it is Pallas who sacrifices you with this wound'.
body: Immolare is a ritual word: to sprinkle the victim with mola salsa (salted meal) and so to sacrifice it. Conington and Nettleship explain 'immolat' as 'as a victim required by justice', and compare 'poenamque inimico ex sanguine sumit' (11.720). The word links the ending to the human victims Aeneas took 'inferias quos immolet umbris' for Pallas' pyre (10.519), and to the treaty sacrifice that began the book. Aeneas presents the act not as his own but as Pallas' vengeance: the repeated name ('Pallas ... Pallas') makes the dead boy the agent. He then 'buries' the sword in Turnus' breast 'fervidus', burning hot. Whether the sacrificial language sanctifies the killing or exposes its savagery is part of the debate about the end of the poem.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 485, note on 12.949
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. immolo

title: The last line of the Aeneid
greek: ast illi solvuntur frigore membra / vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras
short: The poem ends with Turnus' death: his life 'flees with a groan, indignant, to the shades', the same line used for Camilla's death.
body: The line repeats 11.831, the death of Camilla, as Conington and Nettleship note. Servius offers three explanations of 'indignata' (resentful): because after his plea Turnus did not win pardon; because he knew Lavinia would be Aeneas'; or, as with Camilla, because the soul leaves a young body unwillingly, the philosophers holding that the soul departs reluctantly from a body it could still have inhabited by nature's law, and he cites Homer's lines on Patroclus and Hector (Iliad 16.856-7, 22.362-3). The poem ends without a funeral, a wedding or a founding: there is no return to Aeneas' feelings or to the promised peace. This abrupt close, with the victim's resentful soul rather than the victor's triumph, has shaped modern debate about whether the Aeneid celebrates or questions the cost of empire.

sources.cite: Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 12.952
J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 485, note on 12.949-952
